claim: Tasks where success rates fall in the middle range (not near 0% or 100%) provide the most discriminative signal for comparing agent capabilities
quote: Tasks where success rates fall in the middle range (not near 0% or 100%) create meaningful differentiation

claim: SWE-bench dual criterion requires fail-to-pass AND pass-to-pass; agents cannot delete tests to score a pass
quote: you cannot delete the failing test or disable all tests to score a pass

claim: SWE-bench difficulty tiers: easy tasks average 5 lines in 1 file, hard tasks average 56 lines across 2+ files
quote: Easy: average lines changed 5.04, Files modified 1.03; Hard: average lines changed 55.78, Files modified 2.0

claim: Benchmarks sourced from real codebases outperform synthetic puzzles; HumanEval is saturated and no longer discriminates
quote: Unlike HumanEval (164 toy functions, now saturated) or MBPP (basic Python, also saturated), SWE-bench tests whether an agent can solve real software engineering problems in real codebases

claim: Effective challenge specs follow SMART criteria and must include clear direction, measurable evaluation criteria, and real-world constraints
quote: Effective hackathon challenges follow the SMART framework: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound

claim: Spec misalignment is the largest failure mode in end-to-end coding agent benchmarks at 41.86% of all failures; ProjDevBench uses 80% execution and 20% code review scoring
quote: Specification Misalignment (41.86% of failures) - Agents omit critical business logic or misunderstand implementation requirements

claim: Evaluate outcomes not tool call sequences; use pass@k and pass^k metrics for non-deterministic agents
quote: Agents regularly find valid approaches that eval designers didn't anticipate, so rigid step-checking creates brittle tests that penalize creativity unfairly

claim: Effective coding rubrics use 4-6 dimensions on a 1-4 scale combining automated graders for objective criteria with human/LLM review for subjective ones
quote: best practices recommend defining 4–6 core evaluation dimensions such as Correctness, Robustness, Efficiency, Readability, Testing, and Communication, with 3–5 score points

claim: SlopCodeBench structures evaluation as ordered checkpoints pairing specs with test suites, measuring degradation across a run
quote: The benchmark preserves the agent's own code across steps, has evolving specifications across multiple checkpoints, and measures quality at every step

claim: EvoClaw's Milestone Resolve Rate scores whether each ordered checkpoint was reached; Score metric quantifies partial progress within each milestone
quote: the Milestone Resolve Rate assesses whether a milestone was fully resolved while a Score metric quantifies partial progress

claim: LLM judges agree with human reviewers ~85% of the time, higher than inter-human agreement (~81%)
quote: an LLM judge agrees with human reviewers about 85% of the time — higher than the approximately 81% agreement rate between human reviewers themselves

claim: Rubric-based LLM-as-judge evaluation is more reliable when the task is open-ended and the rubric is explicit, criterion-separated, and calibrated
quote: Rubrics improve reliability when the task is open-ended and the rubric is explicit, criterion-separated, and calibrated

claim: HumanEval and MBPP are saturated by 2026 with stagnant performance spreads; contamination from training data is a real risk for common benchmarks
quote: HumanEval and MBPP have low effectiveness scores with stagnant performance spreads, suggesting their focus on function-level algorithms has been neutralized by training data saturation

claim: Consistent environments (same repo snapshot, runtime, lockfile) are prerequisite for meaningful cross-agent comparisons on multi-file feature tasks
quote: Tasks necessitating modifications across various codebase components rather than isolated changes demand contextual understanding of existing code architecture

claim: Scope drift — agents completing a task then fixing unrequested nearby code — complicates scoring and can introduce regressions; use static rubrics for fair head-to-head evaluation
quote: A failure pattern called scope drift occurs when an agent given a specific task completes that task and then, unprompted, decides to also fix something nearby, which can complicate code reviews and introduce unintended regressions
